title: Day 17 of letting an AI trading agent run a small real account: three same-day QQQ calls in the hours before the Fed minutes, all mine, all sold red, and the first one finished in the money
author: Accomplished_Fun_408
selftext:
Disclosure: I work at Flow AI, the company behind Bobby AI, an AI trading agent, and RockFlow, the brokerage the account sits at. My own money, small size, under $2K at risk. Not advice, my own calls.

Days 1 to 17 come from the broker's order export. This is the last replayed day; it goes live from here. Days 1, 5 and 15 are in my post history.

Day 16, Oct 6: all cash since I sold its three positions on Day 15. It proposed nothing. I asked nothing.

Day 17, Oct 7. The Fed's September minutes were due at 2 pm ET and I knew it. Here is what I did before 2 pm.

11:16. One QQQ $757 call expiring that day, $0.66, with QQQ around $755. I asked it first, again. I didn't save the answer, same mistake as the stock buys. 11:22, sold at $0.46. Six minutes, minus $20.

11:46. One $758 call, $0.59. QQQ had climbed to about $756.80 in the twenty minutes since I sold the first one. 11:58, sold at $0.49. Twelve minutes, minus $10.

13:10. The $758 call again, $0.53, QQQ about $757.20. 13:28, sold at $0.47. Eighteen minutes, minus $6.

Thirty-six minutes in the market. Minus $36 before fees, $11.80 in fees, minus $47.80. The fees were a quarter of the loss. Then the minutes came out at 2 pm and QQQ did nothing: $757.37 at 2:10, $757.73 at the close, down 0.25% on the day.



The ledger entry, filled in after the fact with the four fields a commenter gave me on Day 15:

\- Thesis: none written. "QQQ goes up today" is the most I can reconstruct.

\- Max loss: the premium, $66, $59, $53. Each a few percent of the account, so inside what it said it would tolerate by size, outside it by count.

\- Exit rule: none. Each one was sold the first time it was red.

\- What the agent recommended: asked, not saved. On Day 15 its answer was time decay and a few percent at most.

\- Process: 0 for 3. Outcome: the $757 call I dumped at 11:22 finished about $0.75 in the money; sold near the close it would have made about $5 after fees instead of losing $20. The two $758 calls expired worthless, so selling them early saved $96 of the $112 I paid. One early exit cost money, two saved money, and none of the three was a decision.

Oct 8, QQQ fell 1.3%. I was in cash. Nothing I decided put me there.

Scoreboard for the replay, Day 1 to 17. Its three picks, held 10 to 14 days and closed by me: plus $17.99 net on $1,712, 1.05%, against SPY plus 0.17% over the same window. My four options trades: minus $1 before fees, minus $16.73 after. The fees were the loss. Account: plus $1.26.

Live from here. The rules, all of them collected from the comments on Days 1 to 15: every proposal comes with its reason, the one condition that would make it wrong, my one-line reply, and the proposed and confirmed timestamps; every close states a reason unless a stop was set in advance; the same name twice in a week and it has to say what changed; every override goes in the ledger with thesis, max loss, exit rule and what it recommended, scored on process separately from P&L, reviewed after 20 overrides or on Day 90. One post a week.

Question: CPI is tomorrow at 8:30. What's your rule for scheduled-release days, no new positions before the print, smaller size, or nothing special? My record on those days is above.

comments.author: leroylabs
comments.body: My rule would be no discretionary 0DTE entries from 60 minutes before a scheduled release until 15 minutes after it, unless the strategy was explicitly designed and tested for that event. For tomorrow’s 8:30 CPI, Bobby AI should have to classify any proposal as either an event trade or an ordinary signal, then state the expected holding period and invalidation before confirmation. Day 17 shows why: three QQQ calls created $11.80 in fees, while none had an exit rule. Smaller size would limit damage, but it would not fix the missing decision process.

replies.author: Accomplished_Fun_408
replies.body:
Checked the clock against your window. The minutes were at 2:00, so the first two calls, 11:16 and 11:46, were outside 60 minutes and the third, 13:10, was inside. Your rule would have stopped one of three. The other two were plain impatience, which is why the rule I need sits upstream of yours: no discretionary 0DTE entry at all without an exit rule written before the order, and your blackout on top of that.

For CPI tomorrow I'll run your gate as a required answer rather than hope it volunteers one: before I confirm anything it has to label the proposal event trade or ordinary signal, give the expected holding period and the invalidation. Missing any of the three means no order. I'll post what it said, or that it said nothing, in a comment here tomorrow.

One question: does your window cover discretionary closes too, or only entries? On this account the closes are the thing that keeps costing me.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: My rule for release days is to decide before the print, in writing, whether you trade at all: either no new positions inside a set window around the release (for example from 30 minutes before to 15 minutes after), or a fixed smaller size, and then follow it. Spreads and option premiums are usually inflated into the print, so the same trade costs more than on a normal day, which is part of why short-dated calls before a scheduled release are hard to win. Your own record answers it better than opinions can: tag each past trade as release day or normal day and compare the average net result with fees, with the trade count, since 4 trades can't say much yet. Event Cards at Cymetica are one place to look at event-based markets around CPI and Fed releases.
